hook: This is the photograph that made Einstein famous.
narration: This is the photograph that made Einstein famous. May twenty-ninth, nineteen-nineteen. A British astronomer named Arthur Eddington pointed a telescope at a total solar eclipse off the coast of West Africa. Einstein had said that mass curves spacetime, and that starlight grazing the Sun would bend by one point seven five arcseconds. Newton said zero point eight seven. A factor of two. After the eclipse, the photographic plates went home to Cambridge. Eddington and Davidson laid them face to face on a Zeiss measuring engine and tabulated the displacement of fifteen stars by hand. The Sobral plates gave one point nine eight arcseconds, plus or minus zero point one two. Einstein, confirmed. Newton, displaced. Within a week, the New York Times put the words 'Lights All Askew in the Heavens' on its front page. That number is why your phone navigates. SUBSCRIBE for more decoders. beats.text: This is the photograph that made Einstein famous.
May twenty-ninth, nineteen-nineteen. A British astronomer named Arthur Eddington pointed a telescope at a total solar eclipse off the coast of West Africa.
Einstein had said that mass curves spacetime, and that starlight grazing the Sun would bend by one point seven five arcseconds. Newton said zero point eight seven. A factor of two.
After the eclipse, the photographic plates went home to Cambridge. Eddington and Davidson laid them face to face on a Zeiss measuring engine and tabulated the displacement of fifteen stars by hand.
The Sobral plates gave one point nine eight arcseconds, plus or minus zero point one two. Einstein, confirmed. Newton, displaced.
Within a week, the New York Times put the words 'Lights All Askew in the Heavens' on its front page. That number is why your phone navigates.
